newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS - JOHNSON WON'T TRY WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS DOUBLE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS - JOHNSON WON'T TRY WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS DOUBLE.

text.p: Even before the pair of Atlanta gold medals were drapped around his neck, Michael Johnson knew this season would be different.

A single triumph, either at 200 or 400 meters, would be his goal for August's world championships, he had decided, not the historic double he achieved by winning both events at last year's Olympics and at the 1995 world championships.

"I don't want that to become the norm of every championship, to be expected to do both," Johnson said as he prepared for a 200-meter race in Sunday's Prefontaine Classic grand prix meeting in Eugene, Oregon.
Having already made history, "it's not really a lot of appeal to go in there and run the 2 and the 4," the talented Texan said. "I want that to be special, something that I do here and there."
The coming weeks will be far from dull, however, After his Eugene appearance, Johnson will go after a paycheck as unique as his Olympic double.
A tidy $1.5 million will go to the winner of a 150-meter duel between the 200-meter world record holder and Canadian 100-meter world record holder Donovan Bailey in Toronto's SkyDome on June 1.
"Outside of the Olympics it's the biggest, and highest profile event I've ever competed in," said the confident Johnson.

The three-hour programme -- also featuring hurdlers Gail Devers and Ludmila Engquist, pole vaulters Sergei Bubka and Okkert Brits, women's long jumpers Jackie Joyner-Kersee and Heike Drechsler, and high jumpers Charles Austin and Javier Sotomayor in head-to-head competition -- should provide a major boost to track and field in the United States and Canada, Johnson said.
Already there is talk of a U.S. rematch with some pitching the glamour and glitter of Las Vegas as the ideal setting.
Johnson's first objective after Toronto, though, will be deciding whether the 200 or 400 meters will be his choice for this year's U.S. and world championships.

The longer race draws the speculation of many since Johnson already has achieved the ultimate at 200 meters, twice breaking the world record last year, the second time with an astounding run of 19.32 seconds to earn the Olympic gold medal.
The decision, Johnson said, would depend on which race fits his plans not only for this year, but for the long term, which he hopes will include Sydney's 2000 Olympics.
"I would like to break it eventually," he said of Butch Reynolds' 400-meter world record of 43.29 seconds. "But whether it will happen this year I can't say."
The 200-meter record, which Johnson lowered an astonishing 0.4 seconds last year, appears secure. "Outside of myself, I don't see anyone who can run 19.32 right now," he said.
Both the 200 and 400 will dot his European schedule because a mixture of the two seems to help his running in general, Johnson said.
But only on that next "special" occasion, maybe Sydney's Games, will he attempt the double of Atlanta.
"Those two weeks at the Olympics were the biggest accomplishment of my life ... the best dream come true that I have ever had," Johnson said.

"Hopefully other things will happen in my life outside of track that will be just as big, and just as exciting. But to this point, as a 29-year-old single male with no kids, that was the best thing that has ever happpened to me."
